speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF U.S. REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will permit me to make reference to the presence in the gallery today of distinguished representatives of the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States who are here for the purpose of attending the meeting of the Canadian-United States interparliamentary group. I think, for the purpose of the record, I should place on Hansard the names of the various representatives who are here.
The Senate is represented by Hon. George D. Aiken, chairman; Hon. Roman L. Hruska; Hon. Pat McNamara; Hon. Mrs. Maurine B. Neuberger and Hon. Claiborne Pell. The representatives of the House of Representatives are Hon. Cornelius E. Gallagher, chairman; Hon. Laurence Curtis; Hon. William S. Broomfield; Hon. William T. Murphy; Hon. Robert N. Giaimo; Hon. John M. Slack, Jr.; Hon. Harold T. Johnson; Hon. Daniel K. Inouye; Hon. Stanley R. Tupper who, by the way, is a descendant of Sir Charles Tupper, one time prime minister of Canada; Hon. Howard W. Robison and Hon. James Harvey.
I extend on behalf of this house, and I am sure the members of the opposition will join with me, the warmest congratulations and good wishes. Indeed, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) will recall that in the month of January, 1943, for the first time in our history members of the congress of the United States met members of the Canadian parliament and members of the various parliaments of the commonwealth here in Ottawa to discuss those matters that particularly affected the welfare of our respective nations. He knows the close relationship that prevails and which we all hope will continue in the years ahead between the United States and Canada and the other members of the commonwealth.
Then in 1958 this organization had its beginning. As I look back on that beginning I think generally speaking it will be recognized that this interparliamentary group embarked on an uncharted course which held out almost 26207-1-87i
as much prospect of adventure-some predicted misadventure-as did that trip into space the other day by Colonel Glenn. I believe that this interparliamentary group, and what it means in co-operation between our nations, is as important to all of us as any interplanetary activities. In its common dedication to the things in which we believe we are united in freedom.
These gatherings which alternate between Washington and Ottawa provide channels of communication that otherwise would not be available between the lawmakers of our two nations. These meetings permit a review of the ever widening range of our common interests, and these discussions assist us in our consideration of the solution of these problems.
One could say a great deal, but I think the message I am trying to convey could be summarized in a few words. While from time to time we have our differences, the things that unite us, being of the spirit, are becoming stronger with the passing years. What we need is infinite patience, with a full realization of the problems of each other, to the end that in mutual understanding, forbearance and patience we shall strengthen the bonds between our nations and thereby show the rest of the world what can be achieved when independent peoples, each maintaining their own sovereignty, are prepared to join together in peace for the welfare of their respective countries and, indeed, the welfare of all mankind.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF U.S. REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
I would like to echo the words of the Prime Minister in welcoming the members of the Canada-United States interparliamentary committee to Canada. This has been an excellent committee, which has done work of a practical and permanent nature. There are unquestionably important problems to solve between our country and the United States, problems which may cause difficulty and friction; but when we look at what has transpired in the past, and particularly at what took place during the war years between our two countries-I have in mind now our balance of trade payments, the construction of the Alaska highway and the building of the northwest passage-I can come to no other conclusion but that when men of good will and understanding want to solve problems, they can do it. I can remember, too, in those years when there was some difficulty about receiving into the Yukon certain members of the United States army

U.S. Representatives in Gallery because of war regulations. Those members were admitted into Canada by means of an order in council which exempted them under the title of "distinguished citizens".
I should like to mention the St. Lawrence seaway as another example, sir, of the manner in which our problems have been solved, because I had some little experience with that project. There we had difficulties of construction, of costs and of plans and specifications in the international section of the river. I can pay no greater tribute to those from the United States who sat on the opposite side of the table from us than refer to the manner in which they helped, because of their understanding and co-operation, to solve many difficult problems.
I also commend you, sir, for the manner in which you have presided over the deliberations of the Canadian section of this committee and I wish you and those who are associated with you well in your deliberations.

Naturally, I address myself to all members of the committee but especially to Senator Aiken of Vermont, whose state is right next to the province of Quebec with which it has been maintaining good relations for many years.
I ask him to pay our respects to our Franco-American compatriots who live not only in Vermont but in all the states of New England.

Mr. Speaker, as one of the members participating in the particular set of meetings that are going on, speaking on behalf of the members of the New Democratic party may I associate this group wholeheartedly with the remarks of welcome by the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Laurier to the distinguished senators and members of the House of Representatives of the United States who are with us for the sixth meeting of the Canada-United States interparliamentary group.
1 know that our members are unanimously of the opinion that it is impossible to find words to express our appreciation for the hospitality that has been shown to us on previous occasions. The ideas expressed by representatives of the United States are, from our point of view, excellent and the discussions are free and open. Frequently


their ideas have merit. Sometimes we differ with them and I am sure that sometimes they differ with our points of view, but I think agreements which are treasured the most are those agreements which are reached after the expression of differences of opinion.
This interparliamentary group affords an opportunity for the free, frank and fruitful discussion of problems of mutual concern to our respective countries. We trust that this visit will not only increase mutual understanding, but will be enjoyed and remembered by our visitors from the nation to the south. We know that our goal and objectives are the same, namely peace, prosperity and happiness not only for ourselves but for all nations of the world. We are sure these discussions will tend to move us more quickly toward these goals.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON SALE OF VESSELS TO CUBA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address an appropriate question to the Minister of Transport. In view of public interest and reported recent developments in the case of the Canadian National Steamships vessels which were sold to Cuban interests during the Batista regime, which failed to meet their obligations, leaving the ships to rot in Halifax, would the minister bring us up to date on the latest developments and state specifically whether the deal has now been completed to the government's satisfaction and whether any of the vessels are now in use?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON SALE OF VESSELS TO CUBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fleet of eight vessels was sold in August, 1958 to the Banco Cubano del Commercio Exterior of Havana, Cuba, for $2,800,000. The agreement of sale provided for an immediate cash payment of $560,000 with the balance payable in five equal annual instalments of $448,000, with interest on the unpaid balance at 5 per cent per annum. The instalment due in August, 1961 was met in full and the principal outstanding under the agreement has been reduced to $896,000. This balance plus interest continues to be covered by a letter of credit guaranteed by the Bank of America, New York.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The ships having been sold, the government has no knowledge as to whether they are now in use.

the very heavy and continuing impact of the house building and related industries on the national economy, an impact that has been revealed in all its sharpness and clarity by the giant forward steps taken by this government during the years since it assumed office in June of 1957.
It is not my purpose or intention today to review in detail all the developments that have taken place during the past four and a half years as a result of the federal government's interest in and concern with housing. Even a simple chronology of events, a straight recital of new legislation, policy determinations and procedural adjustments, would take more time than I have at my disposal. The events have been many in number and forward thinking in nature, and have arisen out of our forthright common sense approach to the complex problems that have confronted us and out of our ability to adapt to meet changing circumstances. And woven into the whole fabric of housing, bright and chromatic in its colours, has been our resolute determination to assist those Canadians whose needs are most urgent, namely the lower income families of our nation and our senior citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am not going to raise my voice again. There were 115,607 units completed in 1961. The total was slightly below the corresponding figure of 123,757 for 1960, a decline of 6.5 per cent. This year's completions brought the aggregate since 1957 to some 650,000. This means that one out of every six Canadian families is living in a new house built since 1957. My hon. friends can call that anything they like, but it is a magnificent record.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
What effect have these high rates of production had on the market for new housing? As I was able to tell you last September in introducing a measure to amend the National Housing Act, the answer is that there continues to be a satisfactory balance between production and consumption; and that in spite-I am glad to see my hon. friend is here-of the impact of a volume of new 26207-1-88
Supply-Public Works
house construction of this magnitude, output has kept pace with demand but has not been permitted to exceed it. At the end of 1961 the number of completed and unoccupied houses and duplexes in 36 major Canadian urban centres was 4,223, down 5.5 per cent from the figure for December, 1960.
Responsible in part for this encouraging state of affairs is government policy which, while not denying an N.H.A. mortgage loan to any eligible prospective borrower, has controlled the use of public funds for speculative purposes by the approval of C.M.H.C. loans to merchant builders only when the houses for which they are intended have been pre-sold to satisfactory purchasers. As my hon. friends will appreciate, this really worked out well, as the figures must indicate.
Mortgage funds required to finance new National Housing Act residential construction were in substantially better supply during 1961, with life insurance and trust and loan companies continuing to meet the bulk of the need. Of particular interest was the spirited participation of trust companies, whose volume of N.H.A. lending, in terms of dwelling units financed, was almost three times that of their previous record year in 1958, also during the regime of the Diefenbaker government.
Nevertheless, in the virtual absence of loans from the chartered banks the flow of N.H.A. mortgage money was not wholly adequate, and it was supplemented as required by public funds in the form of residual loans by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for which there was a steady demand throughout the year. As hon. members are aware, it has always been our policy to encourage a maximum investment on the part of approved lenders in national housing mortgage loans. Consistent with this policy it has been necessary at the same time to maintain the lowest possible interest rate so that borrowers do not find themselves confronted by unnecessarily excessive costs for the money they have obtained.
I respectfully submit that both these objectives have been attained. Throughout 1961 the N.H.A. interest rate was at a level sufficiently high to be attractive to the approved lenders, but when a continuing flow of new funds seemed assured, at least for the foreseeable future, and the borrowing rate of the government had decreased slightly, it appeared reasonable that the N.H.A. interest rate should be reduced. This action was taken on November 6, 1961 and at the same time interest rates on loans for limited dividend housing, for municipal sewage treatment projects, and for university residences were also lowered.
It is interesting to note that during the year 1961 life insurance, trust and loan companies

Supply-Public Works
were responsible for loans aggregating $452 million, or 62 per cent of total commitments. This figure compares with $232.2 million or 59 per cent of total commitments in 1960. In addition, central mortgage made $271.3 million available from public funds, compared with $161.1 million in 1960. That is a great participation for the crown corporation, $271.3 million, and in all some 64,000 new dwelling units were financed under the N.H.A. Act in 1961. Of these about 63,000 were built with mortgage loans, 38,500 by approved lenders and 24,500 by the corporation. Federal-provincial partnership arrangements accounted for the balance. In 1960 only 37,000 units were financed under the act, just one half of last year's volume.
It is readily apparent that the physical product of the N.H.A. mortgage loans must be, and is, highly significant in terms of employment in the building trades. You may recall that last fall I said each new dwelling unit financed under the N.H.A.-and this is so important, and has been so important in the last five years, in getting Canada out of the recession-involves an average of two and a half man years of employment, on and off site. On this basis N.H.A. lending in 1961 was responsible for more than 160,000 man years of employment, and of these, federal direct lending for more than 61,500 man years.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, you will agree this is a contribution in which we can all justly take pride and satisfaction. Of the total number of housing units built, if we take a rough figure of 125,000 with two and a half man years for each of them, you can see we have an astonishing number of men getting employment in our housing industry. I might add that not content with merely adding to the central mortgage employment opportunities, I and the officials of central mortgage are working closely with my colleague the Minister of Labour to devise new ways and means of attaining an even higher rate of employment in the building industry, particularly in the winter months.
I have told the story of the N.H.A. mortgage lending in 1961 in some detail, and I should now like to make just a brief reference to conventional loans. I am informed that conventional mortgage lending on new housing by the lending institutions was less in 1961 than in the previous year, when loans were approved for 42,000 dwelling units, amounting to $307 million. However, there was a substantial increase in conventional mortgage loans by these lenders on existing dwellings and on non-residential property, with the dollar value rising to $600 million from $484 million in 1960.
A few minutes ago I referred to our unfailing concern with housing for lower income

families and for elderly persons. This concern was again translated into positive action on several fronts in 1961. For example, some 3,300 units of rental accommodation were financed under the limited dividend provisions of the N.H.A., more than double the number approved in the previous year. Of these, about 2,700 were for lower income families and approximately 600 for our senior citizens. All the activity in these sectors took place in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.
In 1961 production of limited dividend rental accommodation brought the aggregate since mid-1957 to more than 18,600 dwelling units and the total loans to an excess of $143 million. I believe you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that this constitutes a satisfying achievement, not merely in terms of numbers but in the knowledge that thousands of Canadian families, husbands, wives and their fine children, and many elderly persons, have been assisted in their search for improved living accommodation, and this after all is the primary consideration and the raison d'etre of the Diefenbaker government.
Nor must we forget the assistance that has also been afforded to borrowers under the act as a result of amendments approved in 1960, when the ratio of loan to lending value was increased to provide higher loans and lower down payments. The maximum N.H.A. loan by regulation was raised and the permissive repayment period was extended, but even that is not the full story. In partnership with the provincial governments we were again active in the field of public housing and in the realm of urban redevelopment, and we are very, very happy to have Ontario taking such an active interest in the public housing program and very happy to have the assistance which their new program promises. In 1961 according to preliminary statistics-and here I should again stress that few of the 1961 figures I am able to provide today are final-[DOT] the construction of more than 900 dwelling units was approved, and the federal share of public housing expenditures totalled nearly $8 million. This brought to almost 4,000 units the number approved since mid-1957, and the total federal share of expenditures in this respect to more than $54.5 million.
Under similar arrangements the development of 855 building lots for sale to home owners was approved during the year, bringing the total number to more than 4,500 since 1957, and the federal share of expenditures required to develop the lots has exceeded $13 million in the same period. Federal contributions toward redevelopment of blighted areas in our cities totalled more than $5 million in 1961. This figure represents federal grants,

less one half of the estimated recovery from the disposal of the cleared lands.
In 1961 grants, which included one of more than $3.6 million to the city of Winnipeg and one in excess of $1 million to the city of Montreal, brought federal contributions since 1957 for these purposes to more than $18 million. I should also mention that grants amounting to some $600,000 have been made since 1957 to municipalities for urban renewal studies, and most hon. members who represent urban districts must know that their particular localities have benefited as a result of this. Of course these urban renewal studies are intended to identify substandard areas and to form proposals for the solution of problems attributable to blight.
I should now like to review briefly two other highly successful provisions of the National Housing Act, two new concepts that were added, hon. members will recall, late in 1960. The first of these has to do with loans for municipal sewage disposal projects. By the way, this is an idea that I received from the backbenchers on the government side, from whom I have obtained so many other ideas on many other subjects.
The primary purpose of this program is, of course, to assist in resolving the problems of water and soil pollution, which had reached alarming proportions in many parts of Canada. Accordingly the government introduced, and parliament approved, legislation providing loans of up to two thirds of the cost of a project; and to encourage municipalities to tackle the job without delay, 25 per cent of the loan and of the interest paid or accrued will be forgiven if the project is completed on or before March 31, 1963, or on that proportion of the project which is completed by that date.
Last year, the first year of operation, no less than 115 municipalities in all our ten provinces obtained 145 loans in an amount of more than $40 million to assist them in the construction or extension of trunk sewage systems or sewage treatment plants. At the year end there were also on hand some 245 preliminary inquiries-think of that-representing a loan potential of an additional $80.6 million.
I am sure the hon. member for St. Denis must regret that the Postmaster General is out of the chamber for a few moments. As another indication of the response to the legislation, loans were made to 78 communities-we will be glad to have the hon. member back-of less than 5,000 population, and of these 63 have less than 2,000 population and 50 less than 1,000. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I am glad to have you back. Were you in Bermuda? You are looking well. As another indication of the response to the legislation, loans were made to 78 communities of less than 5,000 population, and of these 63 have less than 2,000 population and 50 less than 1,000. In most of these smaller communities sewage systems are being provided where they did not exist before and this has also, in many instances, encouraged the installation of public water systems to replace individual wells.
The committee will be glad to know that there was also a most favourable acceptance of N.H.A. loans to universities to assist in the construction of dormitory accommodation for students. Loans in an aggregate amount of more than $20 million were made to 22 universities and colleges for residences to house some 4,300 students. Preliminary applications had also been received at the end of the year from 11 universities which, if approved, could result in loans amounting to $16.7 million that would help to finance accommodation for an additional 4,000 students.
During 1961, too, as hon. members are aware, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation undertook at the government's request to encourage the development of a secondary market for N.H.A. insured first mortgages by offering for sale a part of the portfolio it had acquired as a result of extensive lending operations since 1957. Indicating a growing interest in N.H.A. mortgages as investments, the corporation sold $41 million of its loans to investment dealers, banks and life insurance and trust and loan companies. Proceeds of sales are used to retire corporation debentures held by the federal government. Many of the loans were resold by the purchasers to pension funds, which had not previously included mortgage investments in their portfolios. This is, of course, only a beginning, but we are confident that a market of this kind, stimulated by periodic sales by C.M.H.C., will create not only a more regular but actually a larger demand for N.H.A. mortgages.
As I mentioned last September, we are also appreciative of the responsibilities imposed upon us by the research provisions of the National Housing Act in directing the search for a more attractive, more utilitarian house for Canadian families at a lower cost. I shall not take time to describe in detail the progress being made on this front, except to say that when

I had the privilege last October of taking part in the formal inauguration of field tests of the mark III experimental house at Rockcliffe I was highly impressed by this and other tasks being undertaken by the National House Builders Association and other groups and individuals with financial assistance by the federal government.
In spite of this record of achievement, the highlights of which I have touched upon today, we are still aware that we can learn from experience, that we can benefit from the knowledge of others. We know we can benefit, too, from the knowledge and criticism of hon. members of this committee, including the hon. member for Nipissing. It is for these reasons that we watch closely at all times housing developments in the United States; that we have, indeed, established and are maintaining a close liaison with our contemporaries in that country. But perhaps the older cultures have even more lessons for us, and I counted it a privilege last autumn when I was able to make an all too brief visit to Europe for the purpose of looking into the house construction and financing techniques being used in some countries over there. Later, as hon. members know, I attended an important conference in southeast Asia, and again I was able to see in another dimension the latest developments in the housing field.
At my suggestion the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and three of his senior officials subsequently undertook a more detailed examination of housing developments in England, Scotland, Sweden and Holland. The primary purpose of the study by Dr. Bates and his party was to inquire into the methods of producing housing in those countries and examine the ways in which housing is financed and subsidized.
I have reached the end of my observations on the housing situation in 1961 and in the years since 1957. It may be asked-and it is a proper question-what of the immediate future? What is 1962 likely to have in store for us? I shall not be so rash as to hazard a precise estimate of the number of new housing starts; there are too many imponderables, too many world uncertainties, too many guesses entailed. However, I will say that if only because of the substantial carry-over from 1961, amounting to some 74,000 units, we are confident of another substantial volume of housing investment in 1962. Furthermore, should the number of starts also show an increase over 1961, the investment increment would naturally be of even greater magnitude.
That summarizes the picture of housing as we see it at the present time.

I shall be glad to find that out for the hon. gentleman. I will have the figures available when we are going over the items. I shall be very pleased to do that.
Now may I discuss briefly some features of the departmental activities during 1961-62, and outline certain points of interest in our plans for the coming fiscal year. The total appropriation which is requested in the 196263 public works estimates is $217,451,000. Of the total amount requested, $200,226,000 is for the activities of the department as such. The remainder consists of $660,000 required by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and $16,565,000 for the national capital commission. The accounts for the present fiscal year are, as hon. members are aware, still active; and while it is not possible at this time to give precise figures on expenditures, I expect the usual high percentage of the funds appropriated will be spent. Usually the estimates of the Department of Public Works come down in the committee much later than this.
I should like now to report on the budding construction activities of the department. In order to provide needed accommodation for government services across Canada, construction was begun on a number of important buildings during the year. These included a building for the Queen's printer in Halifax, Nova Scotia, $248,700; a public building in Kentville, Nova Scotia, $368,936; in Montreal, Quebec, a building for the Department of Veterans Affairs, $1,063,400; as well as a building for the western zone office of the unemployment insurance commission, $455,000; St. Hyacinthe, Quebec, a public building valued at $440,758; in Ottawa, Ontario, alterations and improvements valued at $5,088,000 were begun on the west block as well as a computer centre for the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, $1,738,488; in Etobicoke, Ontario, a new public building, $179,429; Lacombe, Alberta, a public building, $147,794; in Prince Rupert, British Columbia, a new public building, $703,524 and in Vancouver, British Columbia, a building to house the unemployment insurance commission and postal station "C", $729,000.
In addition to these projects begun during the year, construction continued on other major projects such as additions to public buildings in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and Moncton, New Brunswick, and the new postal terminal in Quebec city. Here in Ottawa I can

point to the completion of the new building for the Post Office Department at Confederation Heights and continuing work on the new building for the headquarters staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare in Tunney's pasture. In London, Ontario, there was a new postal terminal; in Toronto the Arthur Meighen building was opened; in Winnipeg the new unemployment insurance building was completed; and in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan and Penticton, British Columbia, new public buildings were completed.
During the year the department continued to assist the winter works program through the construction of standard post office buildings in smaller communities across Canada. I will not bother to give a list of these locations, since they have already appeared in Hansard on February 9 of this year.
Turning now to the harbours and rivers work, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the more noteworthy of the many projects currently in progress. For example, in St. John's, Newfoundland, work continued on the complete reconstruction of one of North America's oldest harbours. At Baie Comeau, along the province of Quebec's flourishing north shore, the department, in conjunction with private interests and the provincial government, is undertaking a major expansion of harbour facilities. Important harbour improvements are also under way at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Cornwall, Oshawa and Port Credit, Ontario. In Toronto harbour, work on the extention to the shipping channel and for the provision of additional seaway berthage continued, and these facilities are expected to be available in time for the 1963 shipping season. Work also continued during the year at the lakehead on the construction of new terminal facilities capable of accommodating ocean going vessels. At Nanaimo, British Columbia and Grand Manan, New Brunswick, important wharf projects were begun.
Before dealing with the trans-Canada highway I will continue to review what has been accomplished with respect to harbour improvements and repairs. During the current year major harbour improvement and repair projects were completed at Hamilton, Ontario and continued at Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, and Pointe au Pere, Quebec and at Pictou, Nova Scotia. A breakwater extension in the St. John area at Negro Town point in New Brunswick and the reconstruction of the assembly wharf at Port Alberni, British Columbia, were completed. Work also continued on the million dollar water supply system to serve the various federal communities in the vicinity of Fort Churchill.


And now a word about the trans-Canada highway. As hon. members know, the province of Quebec became a party to the trans-Canada highway agreement on October 27, 1960. To my friend the hon. member for Levis may I say that we welcome the inclusion of that province. All ten provinces now participate in this grand design.
Under the agreement with the provinces, provision is made for federal participation in the construction of the highway across each of the ten provinces. The total value of the work approved to date is estimated at $689,823,000, of which Canada's share is estimated at approximately $400 million. Payments during the present fiscal year to date approximate $31 million. The total mileage of the highway, exclusive of 140 miles through the national parks, totals 4,719 miles, of which 2,995 miles have been completed under the agreement. Adding some 1,000 miles of the highway which were paved prior to the passing of the act, nearly 4,000 miles of the highway now have a paved surface. The sections of the highway through the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta are practically completed, and the remaining provinces are making every effort to complete the highway before December 31, 1963, although completion is doubtful in Newfoundland and Quebec.
The construction of the sections of the highway through the national parks is a federal responsibility. Expenditures on this account to date total $68,247,000, of which $5,875,000 covers expenditures during the present fiscal year.
I did not hear what the figure of $68,247,000 related to.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
That relates to national parks, which are a federal responsibility. It is expected that all major work, with the exception of additional snow sheds in the Glacier park and final course paving in the Terra Nova, Glacier and Revelstoke parks will be completed before September of this year. The work with respect to Glacier park is a tremendous undertaking and far more difficult than we anticipated. The Glacier and Revelstoke national parks section is part of the Rogers pass route through the Rocky mountains, and is the last major gap in the whole trans-Canada route. It is expected to be declared officially open this fall, which means that for the first time it will be possible to travel the whole trans-Canada route from coast to coast. This will be properly celebrated by the presence of the Prime Minister, who will officially open the trans-Canada highway in Rogers pass, British Columbia, in September of this year. He will be joined there by all ten provincial premiers and by

as many hon. members of the government as are able to attend. I trust that if there are any members of the opposition parties left at that time, as many as possible will attend.
I come now to the department's program for 1962-63. Hon. members will note that the number of large new items included in the estimates indicates that activities of the department will continue at a high level in the months to come.
I should like first of all to consider some of the major projects planned for the Ottawa area. At the Confederation Heights development on Riverside drive, plans are being prepared for two new buildings to house three government departments, one for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Department of Forestry and the other for the Department of Transport. Both will be imposing structures and will complement the over-all scheme of government buildings in the area. Construction is expected to start during the coming year. If any hon. members have a spare moment I urge that they visit Confederation Heights and examine the magnificent development that has taken place there in the last year or two.
Of special interest, I think, is the fact that in the new northern affairs and national resources building, the use of Eskimo art for decorative purposes will be employed and so reflect its close association with the north and northern development. The exterior of the forestry wing will conform to the northern affairs building, but the interior will feature a maximum use of Canadian wood materials.
The transport building will be an imposing high-rise edifice providing the focal point of the whole development. With the completion of these two buildings, along with the new proposed building to house the head office of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, construction in Confederation Heights will be complete. There will remain only the landscaping then, to transform the area into one of the finest collection of government administration buildings to be found in any capital in the world.
Work will also begin this summer on Canada's new national library and archives, which is to be erected on the site of the No. 1 temporary building. Tenders for the building, including demolition of No. 1 temporary building, are to be called this summer to enable work to begin in July, at which time the taxation branch offices in No. 1 temporary building will have been moved to new quarters at Tunney's pasture. Excavation work will begin immediately and is scheduled for completion sometime in 1963, when the actual

construction will begin. The completed building will be open to the public by 1967, in time for Canada's centennial celebrations. Also due to get under way this year is the site development for the mines branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys on the Corktown road location.
I am certain that hon. members are interested in learning of the building construction projects scheduled by the department for other parts of the country. I shall therefore give a brief resume of some of the major projects. They are:
Newfoundland: Additions and alterations are to be made to the public building at Corner Brook.
Nova Scotia: New public buildings will be erected at Shelburne, Springhill and Sydney Mines as well as new unemployment insurance commission headquarters in Halifax.
New Brunswick: New buildings are planned at Edmundston and Sussex.
Quebec: Two new postal buildings and an unemployment insurance commission zone office will be built in Montreal, while federal buildings are scheduled for Grand'Mere, Ste. Genevieve de Pierrefonds and Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere.
Ontario: Public buildings are planned for Arnprior, Brockville, Fort William, Georgetown, Midland, Strathroy, Sudbury and Waterloo.
Manitoba: New buildings will be constructed at Boissevain and Fort Garry.
Saskatchewan: New public buildings at Shellbrook and Duck Lake.
Alberta: New federal buildings will be constructed at Calgary and High Prairie.
British Columbia: New buildings will be constructed at Burns Lake, North Surrey and a building in Vancouver to accommodate unemployment insurance commission offices and postal station "C" will be completed.
Yukon and Northwest Territories: A public building is planned for Hay River.
It is anticipated that the program of erecting standard post offices in the smaller centres across Canada as an aid to winter work will be continued next winter. Present plans call for a program roughly the same size as undertaken this winter.
Considering plans for harbours and rivers during the 1962-63 fiscal year, the department expects to continue with work currently under way at a number of major Canadian ports, as well as to make a start on projects which, when completed, will be of great importance to the Canadian economy as a whole. The extensive harbour improvements at St. John's, Newfoundland, will be continued, as will the harbour improvement projects at Baie Comeau and Pointe au Pere, Quebec.

In Toronto harbour the ship channel extension will be completed and major dredging projects will be continued. Major work including dredging will be undertaken in the Hamilton harbour. The new terminal facilities at the lakehead will be completed and placed in service later this summer. This means that Canada's most inland port will be one of the most modem in the world for handling package freight cargo.
Some of the other major projects to be undertaken during the coming fiscal year are as follows:
Newfoundland: The dredging of a number of high spots and the widening of the channel at Catalina will be undertaken. Major wharf reconstruction and extension work is slated for Old Perlican and Marystown. A new 100-foot long L-shaped wharf will be constructed at Piccadilly. Wharf construction and extension work will be undertaken at Ship Cove to provide improved facilities.
Nova Scotia: A new breakwater wharf is planned for Chapel cove. The existing breakwater at Freeport will be extended some 600 feet. At Pinkney Point a new breakwater will be constructed while at Walton the existing wharf will be replaced. It is also expected that reconstruction of pier "C" at Pictou will be completed during the year. Harbour improvements are planned for Inverness in Cape Breton.
Price Edward Island: A U-shaped breakwater landing will be constructed at Egmont bay, while extensive harbour improvements will be undertaken at Summerside and Al-berton.
New Brunswick: Major harbour improvement projects are scheduled for Botsford, Lameque, and Malloch Beach. In Saint John extensive dredging and a further breakwater extension are planned.
Quebec: At Havre Aubert, large dredging operations will be continued and a start will be made on the construction of a new deep water wharf. Wharf reconstruction will begin at Riviere au Tonnerre and Les Eboule-ments. At Matane and Portneuf large projects are contemplated.
Ontario: Large new harbour projects are scheduled to provide improved facilities at Goderich, Leamington, Port Credit and Sarnia.
Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Northwest Territories:	New wharf facilities will be
undertaken at Barron river, Jan lake and Pelican Narrows as well as major reconstruction of the wharf at Cambridge bay.
British Columbia: A new boat harbour to accommodate a large number of fishing boats is being planned for Nanaimo. An important new ferry terminal is being planned at Prince Rupert to accommodate the proposed ferry

which will operate between Prince Rupert, B.C. and several points along the Alaskan panhandle.
In the field of bridge construction, I am pleased to report good progress on a number of projects. The bridge between Campobello island, N.B., and Lubec, Maine, will be completed and open to traffic in the coming year. Also scheduled for completion this year is the new low level bridge over the Burlington canal.
Hear, hear.

In those years he will require more bedrooms and larger facilities than at any other period. When he has paid for his house in 20 or 25 years his children will have grown up and left home and in his old age he may be left with a white elephant instead of a comfortable cottage in which to spend his years of retirement.
I am not an architect but I feel the government could give consideration to what has been done by some municipalities in providing school buildings. I have visited schools in Toronto. Parts of the schools are portable and can be dismantled a room at a time to meet the fluctuating needs of the school children. Additions can be made to the schools when the need demands. The suburbs have fluctuating populations and there is not always a constant proportion of young people.
Perhaps houses could be built in a similar manner so that they could be expanded or contracted as the need of the family unit changed. Consideration should be given to this project.
May I call it five o'clock.

If hon. members will look at section 4, I think they will agree with me that it authorizes-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ELECTORAL DISTRICTS IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I shall be very pleased to read the section. Section 4 provides as follows:
4. Section 9 of the Canada Elections Act is amended by adding thereto the following subsection :
"(8) In the electoral district of Northwest Territories the returning officer, with the written authorization of the chief electoral officer, may appoint more than one election clerk and establish, if necessary, an office in each locality designated by the chief electoral officer, and may delegate, in writing, to any such election clerk appointed his powers of selecting and appointing enumerators and deputy returning officers and of selecting polling places."
Hon. members will observe that the first three sections are an amendment to the Representation Act which does not provide for the expenditure of any funds but is an act to deal with representation and electoral districts. On the other hand, section 4 provides for an amendment to the Canada Elections Act under which provision is made for payment of the expenses of elections. The problem I wish to present to the house is that section 4 appears to authorize an expenditure of public funds. For the convenience of hon. members who wish to look into the matter I may say that the requirements with respect to bills which authorize an expenditure of public funds are found in section 54 of the British North America Act which states in part as follows:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue... to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General-
That is part of the section. Then our standing order 61 implements that statutory provision. References to the practice will be found in Beauchesne's fourth edition, in citations 243, 245 and 355. In determining whether any particular legislation appropriates money

Representation Act
within the meaning of these provisions the issue is not the amount of money but whether there is an appropriation of public funds. I cannot but come to the conclusion that section 4 authorizes the expenditure of public funds.
If that would stand in the way of the progress of the bill, it might be that the issue could be dealt with either by amendment or, if it is desired to proceed with the bill, this difficulty could be rectified by deferring it until a resolution has been brought in. It would not be proper for this bill to be read a third time and passed, thus setting a precedent which would stand in the future against the well known constitutional practice that no public funds are ever appropriated, involving as they do taxation, without the house having an opportunity to consider the matter in the resolution stage in committee before the bill itself is presented.
It would be in order, of course, to refer the bill back to the committee with instructions to delete clause 4. It may be that the Canada Elections Act, as it stands, would be the means of providing the money necessary for the implementation of clauses 1, 2 and 3 of the bill. If so, then clauses 1, 2 and 3 could be made effective even if clause 4 were deleted. If the Canada Elections Act does not have these enabling provisions, then it is all the more evident that the proposed amendment to the Canada Elections Act contravenes our practice.

REVISION OF GRADES RESPECTING RAPESEED AND MUSTARD SEED
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-15, to amend the Canada Grain Act (rape-seed and mustard seed).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that last session I introduced Bill No. C-130, to amend the Canada Grain Act. The wording of Bill No. C-15 which is before the house for discussion at the present time is very similar to that of the bill I introduced last session.
Hon. members will know that Canada is best known in the commercial markets of the world for the high quality of her grains, particularly wheat. The purpose of this bill to amend the Canada Grain Act is to bring grains such as rapeseed and mustard seed to the same high standard as other Canadian grains. Ninety to 95 per cent of all the rapeseed grown in this country is exported, and it is imperative that the quality of this grain be of the highest standard that we are able to achieve.
The amendment before the house proposes to revise the present statutory grades for rapeseed to meet present day trade requirements. It is in conformity with the suggestion of the board of grain commissioners for Canada to have the Canada Grain Act reclassified in accordance with schedules A and B of the bill. It also meets with the full approval of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), under whose jurisdiction fall the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners for Canada. I am sure it will also meet with the approval of hon. members of this house. Schedules A and B are based on the recommendations of the chief grain inspector for the board of grain commissioners and are in compliance with the export requirements contained in stipulations with regard to maximum percentage of foreign materials, degree of soundness and standard of cleanliness.
Clause 2 of the bill will change the definition of the grades of domestic mustard seed from the present commercial definition to a statutory definition. The committee on western grain established commercial grades for domestic mustard seed on November 4, 1953. These grades have now been revised to meet trade requirements, and the effect of this amendment is to raise these revised commercial grades to the level of statutory grades.
Canada Grain Act
At their annual meeting the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates also asked the board of grain commissioners to include the presence of mustard in rapeseed as a factor in grading. Mr. Speaker, it is not now a factor except for a declaration as to mustard seed content when rapeseed is exported. It is generally accepted in the trade that the presence of more than 2 per cent of mustard in a rapeseed sample reduces its value as a source of edible oil. The identification of mustard in rapeseed-which are similar in size and colour-requires special equipment.
I must inform the house that unless steps are taken to change the grading to that spelled out in my bill, mustard may ruin the rapeseed crop, and thus growers of rapeseed will be faced with a loss of vital markets unless they produce a crop free of mustard seed. If mustard seed is allowed to become an impurity in rapeseed, processors could not hope to use it for making edible oils.
The menace of mustard contamination of prairie rapeseed crops is now recognized by the three western provinces as being extremely serious. In southern Alberta mustard has been grown for many years, and it should be left to these places to grow all the mustard seed that can be sold. There is no need to extend the mustard acreage into Saskatchewan. This is completely unnecessary, because we could sell to the United States and other countries all the mustard they need from the crops produced in southern Alberta.
Of course, we are aware of the fact that some commercial interests are now actively encouraging the growing of mustard throughout Saskatchewan by offering contracts which might sound attractive to farmers, but the farmers are uninformed about the dangers involved. If we ignore these threats to our rapeseed crops in the west and attempt to grow mustard and rapeseed in the same areas, then I say, Mr. Speaker, that we would be killing the goose that lays the golden egg, as far as rapeseed producers are concerned. Wild mustard alone, without any additional trouble from the two types of tame mustard, would be capable of killing the market for rapeseed to be used for the manufacture of margarine or for export.
Mr. Frank Mohler of the seed growers of Maymont, this year's president of the Saskatchewan branch of the Canadian seed growers' association, expressed concern about this matter and said that growers of rapeseed faced a loss of vital markets unless they took pains to produce a crop free of mustard seeds, both wild and tame.
Dr. H. R. Sallans, oilseed chemistry specialist in the prairie regional laboratory of the national research council in Saskatchewan,

Canada Grain Act
urges that rapeseed and mustard be kept separate and be grown in different fields and different districts.
Dr. Sallans expressed concern that contamination of the seeds of these two crops would affect the marketing potentialities of both. He firmly agreed with a statement made by Mr. F. Mohler, president of the Saskatchewan branch, Canadian seed growers' association, that if a district wished to keep on growing rapeseed it should give up all intention of dabbling in mustard production.
World production of rapeseed in 1961 is believed to have reached an all time high, exceeding for the first time the pre-war average level. It is estimated that the world production of rapeseed is 4.3 million short tons, some 7 per cent more than in 1960 and almost one third more than the 1950-54 average. Virtually all of the rapeseed grown in North America is produced in Canada, namely, a near record of 745,000 acres.
According to Mr. R. E. Merry, president of the institute of edible oilfoods, oilseed production on the prairies could expand to occupy at least 1,500,000 acres, if Canada is to meet her domestic needs and fill the potential demand for rapeseed abroad.
The publication Foreign Trade issued this month by the federal Department of Trade and Commerce, indicates that the future prospects for marketing Canadian rapeseed and mustard seed appear good. The publication also forecasts that the common market countries will provide an expanding outlet for Canadian oilseeds. Canadian exports of oilseeds in 1960 are such as to indicate that both rapeseed and mustard seed have considerable export value. In that year, total exports of rapeseed amounted to $13,240,000, and exports of mustard seed to $2,604,000. Japan and Italy were Canada's best customers for rapeseed.
Hon. members will be aware of the fact that last fall a Canadian oilseed trade mission went to Europe. After two months touring, the members of the mission returned to Canada and reported on what they had seen. The tour was organized by the Department of Trade and Commerce under the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). The government chose men to make up the trade mission who not only knew the oilseed industry but had a personal interest in it. The six nations toured were Great Britain, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy and West Germany. Here are the mission's general conclusions:
The general improvement in economic conditions in western Europe will result in a continuing increase in the consumption of the products of oil seeds. The consumption of fats and oils will steadily increase in those countries, Holland, Belgium, west Germany and Britain, where present

consumption is at a high level. In Italy and France, a sharp increase is envisaged as their consumption is expected to rise sharply to approach the same per capita level as that in the other four countries.
If the proposals for oilseeds, fats and oils in the common market are adopted, a greater potential will exist for increased marketings of oilseeds and oilseed meals in the EEC countries. The proposed tariffs on oils will have the effect of switching some of the trade in oils to oilseeds.
A market for rapeseed exists in all of the countries visited, providing Canadian prices are competitive with those charged for other oilseeds.
The mission made the following recommendations, and I should like to stress their importance:
1.	Consideration should be given to amending the grading nomenclature of rapeseed to read No. 1 Canada rapeseed, No. 2 Canada rapeseed, No. 3 Canada rapeseed etc. Rapeseed containing in excess of some minimum quantity of mustard seed should be degraded.

2.	Consideration of a government agency issuing an export certificate of mustard content in rape-seed upon loading in a Canadian port.
3.	Consideration of a government agency issuing an export certificate of oil content for all oilseeds upon loading in a Canadian port.
Here again I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that rape-seed and mustard seed are very similar in size, colour and weight. 5.	Every effort should be made to contain Canada's mustard seed crop and to inform Canadian growers of the disastrous effects of the mixture of rapeseed and mustard seed upon export sales of rapeseed.

Before the house rose for the recess I was mentioning the fact that there seemed to be a need for a change in the requirements particularly of young people, in the field of national housing. I had indicated that there was a period in which when income was low there was a need for increased facilities and that in later years, when the mortgage was paid off, many of the homes that had been necessary for the young family were not necessarily satisfactory for the retired family. I had suggested that some consideration should be being given now in the form of a study in order to find out whether there is not a better way of solving this particular aspect of the housing problem.

Certainly this situation is developing in many of our cities where it is not necessarily advantageous to own a house at all or it may be much wiser to rent the type of accommodation that is necessary.
This is being done in some the cities through the co-operation of some of the municipalities and the federal and provincial governments in order to allow people to rent homes according to their requirements for the number of children they have and taking into consideration their wage structure and the money available to that family. It may mean that those with a high income will be obliged to pay a much higher rent for the same accommodation than would be paid by workers with a low rate of pay. This may raise the general problem whether or not we have not bent over backwards in Canada, because of our free enterprise background, our pioneering spirit, in the fact that we have jealously guarded this business of house ownership. Certainly they fostered the idea of house ownership. It may be the situation that in years to come it may be advantageous for the government to know whether it would be wise to use rental systems, particularly for low wage earners or low cost rental projects. Some day it may be true that it is not advantageous to buy a house, to make the payments on a house over a very long period of time, and that these houses may be government owned, municipally owned or owned cooperatively by the municipalities and the governments, where the financing can be spread out over an even greater period of time than 25 years.
As we all know, there are in existence now many homes which are serving their occupants very well and which have been built over a period of 60 years or 70 years and in some cases over 100 years, with modifications, of course. This was pointed out quite strongly by Mr. A. C. Ashforth, president of the Toronto-Dominion bank, in an article which appeared in the Prince Rupert daily News of December 6, 1960. With a 35 year mortgage ... the principal repayments for some years will be less than normal depreciation. Apparently the government expects inflation to continue in the housing market.
He goes on to point out that these houses in 10 years may be worth less than the payments that will still be owing on them. He then goes on to say this:
We need to consider if we are not building the wrong kind of houses, for the wrong reasons, in the wrong places, designed for the wrong people, at the wrong time.
Present policy directs N.H.A. financing into new houses and refuses to extent any aid to people buying existing houses. It drives young families into new houses and pushes them into the suburbs

With the one exception I have mentioned, the officials of the department have always been very courteous and always know what they are talking about. I have been to see them on a number of occasions about matters in my riding, and I believe the department has capable officials who are doing a very good job and who should be given credit for it. However, I think the minister will agree with me in saying that it is never so good that it cannot be better. For these reasons I have raised the problems I raised today.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, first of all, I should like to commend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) for having replaced all signs inside the parliament buildings and on nearby buildings by bilingual ones. The purpose of this step is to show to the Canadian people and foreign visitors that there are two official languages and racial groups in Canada. Moreover, following requests made by members of the house and

representatives of the people, he pursued the task undertaken when he had bilingual signs put on all buildings in the national capital.
Mr. Chairman, some time ago, I asked the minister to make a survey in regard to the dredging of L'Assomption river from Le Gardeur de Repentigny bridge to the city of Joliette. The dredging of that river is essential to the economy of the district.
Mr. Chairman, after that project has been examined by the senior officials of the Department of Public Works, I wonder if it would not be necessary for the provincial and federal authorities to come to an agreement in view of the fact that, in the province of Quebec, non-navigable waters come under the Quebec streams commission. I would appreciate such an examination being undertaken as soon as possible by the engineers of the Department of Public Works-who, I am glad to say, are most competent-so that this project may be carried out shortly if it comes under the federal authorities or so that negotiations may be opened between the provincial government and the department for the purpose of reaching an agreement in that connection.
That is a joint program.

I mean while respecting provincial autonomy instead of flouting provincial rights, as you did for 20 years.
Mr. Chairman, please excuse me for this digression. I should not bother to reply to one who was of no value to his party when they were in power. He was here for 20 years without uttering a single word. Today, he is completely changed, he is not the same man. I am sure that the Canadian people will see to it that he is eliminated along, with his friends, for another 20 years, which should enable the Liberal party to amend itself and to obtain better men for the future.
With Maurice Sauve, what a chance they have.

Mr. Chairman, I know that the federal government is contributing, on the average, 50 per cent to the construction cost of the trans-Canada highway. This highway will run through the province of Quebec, and there is a strong possibility that it will pass on the south shore. The north shore of the St. Lawrence river, that is from Joliette to Trois Rivieres is one of the richest regions of the province of Quebec.

In the first place, it is one of the oldest regions and is also tremendously rich in woodland. Moreover, its land and water wildlife is most interesting, and Montreal sportsmen go fishing and hunting in the region north of Montreal, in some areas of my constituency of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and in the constituency of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere. They even build summer camps in those areas.
Consequently, and in accordance with representations made by the mayors of the Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm riding, that is from L'Assomption to Trois Rivieres, I ask the minister whether the government could not consider the advisability of running the trans-Canada highway through our region, extending the metropolitan boulevard to Trois Rivieres and thence towards the south shore, if advisable.
I know that Mr. Mongrain, the mayor of Trois Rivieres is entirely of the same opinion, like the mayor of the town of Joliette and all the mayors in that area who fear economic difficulties. One must recognize that this $150 million highway is some kind of a door opened to industries. I am wondering whether the government of the province of Quebec, who is responsible for the route, will decide that the trans-Canada highway is to be built on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river rather than on the south shore, to bring industrial development to those areas. Otherwise it should announce without delay its intention of building a highway on the north shore.
I would not want the Joliette area and the northern part of the province of Quebec to be pictured as some underdeveloped country. I do hope, Mr. Chairman, that the government of Quebec will not delay progress and will make an affirmative reply in the interests not only of the people in Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, but in the whole province.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to know if the minister has received many requests from Canadian municipalities, particularly those in Quebec, about the construction of sewage treatment plants. It would be advantageous on many counts for the Canadian municipalities to seize the opportunities offered them by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I feel the solution of this problem is now essential.
The chambers of commerce and other
organizations are paying a great deal of attention to the matter. I would be very happy, Mr. Chairman, if the minister would tell us whether he has received any request
Supply-Public Works
from the various provinces and especially whether he has received any from the province of Quebec.
Before dealing with the remarks made this afternoon by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), I would like to reply to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon).
It is not necessary to reply to him.

He would like to see the
trans-Canada highway-
Not necessarily another road, if possible.

-pass through the constituency of Joliette, now that the laying out has been made, chosen and decided. I surely think that the hon. member preaches in the wilderness. He should have made up his mind before 1960, when the construction of the trans-Canada highway was just being started. He then could have had a chance of having it go through his hometown.
The laying out of the trans-Canada highway was done by the former administration.

I shall not spend any more time on the questions asked by the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I am going to deal with the speech made by the minister this afternoon. In fact, he started it with a stormy tone of voice. Happily no scuffle resulted from it. The minister must agree that he personally through his remarks aggravated the house members. He pointed out that only a few members were sitting on the opposition benches but he had not looked on the government side where there were only about 45 members present at that time.
Out of 206.

You have already been defeated by one vote when you were in office.
Mr. Pallet!: They were 80.
You see double.

Privately, the minister is congenial, he is a good chap. But as soon as he rises to speak in the house or elsewhere in
public, his attitude changes entirely.

So does Mr. Lesage's.

Supply-Public Works

I said that when the minister rises in the house it seems that his attitude changes. He has a knack for aggravating his listeners. It seems that he does this in order to distract our attention and thus prevent us from noticing that he is overstating the facts. The minister talked about the various activities of his department and devoted much of his speech to housing.
He reviewed the measures taken by his government under that act. He gave us interresting statistics about the houses built and the amounts invested. But he was modest, because he could have mentioned that the National Housing Act was enacted by a Liberal government and expanded, only, by the present government, which is trying to extend its scope to all the citizens of Canada.
If such was the case, the government failed to achieve its aim. As the hon. minister knows, I represent a Montreal constituency. And the housing statistics for the city of Montreal do not agree with those the minister gave us this afternoon.
Although the minister lives in Toronto-I do not envy him-he must not forget that Montreal is the largest city in Canada and that it does keep statistics too.
The minister gave us, this afternoon, statistics for the whole of Canada. I can tell him that there is an area in Canada where things are not going so well, and that is the city of Montreal.
This afternoon the minister told us that construction started on 125,767 houses in 1961, an increase of 15 per cent over 1960. However, in Montreal, during the first seven months of 1960, housing starts totalled only 8,844 compared to 12,187 during the same period in 1959.
In 1961, the number of building permits in Montreal decreased by one third compared with 1960, and in 1960 it had decreased in comparison with 1959.
The year 1961, which just ended, ranks eighth for the total value of construction, the record year being 1959 with the building of the Dorchester street skyscrapers, in Montreal. The year 1960 came fourth.
This afternoon, the minister stated that during 1961, 3,300 housing units had been built by limited dividend housing companies, of which 2700 were for low income families. I regret that he was not able to give us statistics for each province. However, I can say that very few low rental units have been built in Montreal.
At the present time, apartment houses are being built in Montreal, which are of little value for low income families.
I would be remiss if I did not point out to the minister the cause of the decline in the construction industry in Montreal. There is only one cause and it is that lots or building sites have reached a very high price.
It is true, as the minister pointed out, that housing construction plays an important part in the economy of the nation. In fact, activity in the building trade is a sign of prosperity because all trades are employed.
However, since 1957, while this government has allocated millions to housing, the price of lots has gone up sharply, and a large number of building contractors had to quit that trade, being unable to sell their houses because they had to ask for a price that the buyer could not afford.
The minister stated this afternoon that one family out of seven is living in a new dwelling. That may be true, but I can tell him that it is not the case in the city of Montreal.
The result is, Mr. Chairman, that, with lots being priced too high, single family properties are out of reach for workers and white-collar people. I daresay that one with a $6,000 to $7,000 yearly income and a family of two or three children also finds himself in that category.
Since the minister referred to low cost dwelling units, I hope he will take into consideration the request he received from the mayor and the chairman of the executive council of Montreal for a housing project, under section 6 of the act, on the St. Sulpice Domain and Trinitaires boulevard, in Ville Emard.
The plan submitted by the Montreal municipal authorities was designed to house civic employees. I do hope that the minister will give an affirmative reply.
Newspapers have mentioned that the minister was opposed to these projects because he had been told that there were too many empty units in the city of Montreal. That statement is partly true. However, the apartments which are unoccupied are not one family units but mostly small units of three or four rooms in apartment buildings unsuitable for large families.
Because of the high cost of land, apartment buildings have been built for the past two or three years, to cover entire city lots in Montreal leaving no space back or front. Needless to say, those buildings are not fit for workers with children.

I should like to make one last remark to the minister concerning the research to be carried out on public housing and community planning, under section 5 of the act. This afternoon, he told us that his department is continuing its research in the field of urban housing districts. I note however, on page 363 of his estimates, that the item of $1,649,000 we were asked to vote last year, does not appear this year. Yet, research is very important in this field. Regulations should be enacted, with the co-operation of provincial and municipal authorities, for the guidance of the building industry and for the classification and development of land.
In this respect, X should like to draw the minister's attention to a report which was published in the January 19, 1961 issue of La Presse, during the conference of the home builders' association which was held in Montreal, under the chairmanship of Mr. John Parkin, of Toronto. The report recommended the establishment of a Canadian research institute on urban centres:
The establishment of a Canadian institute of urban area development would be of immense value not only for the building Industry, but also for the general economy of Canada. The creation of such an organization is essential to put an end to land speculation and bring a necessary orderliness in the many housing development projects to be carried out in future years.
Further on, it is stated:
Mr. Parkin feels that it is abnormal for one of the largest industries in this country, the building industry, not to have as yet established its own research centre. Starting from a recent report prepared by the Canadian architectural institute, Mr. Parkin broadly defined the functions of such an organization. It should first of all offer guidance to the building industry throughout Canada, indicating what type of housing would meet the requirements of the Canadian people. It then could deal with land classification and with its development. In a word it could study from an economic viewpoint those districts and urban centres which are developing, in order to regulate their expansion.
Mr. Chairman, I pointed out a moment ago to the hon. minister that if housing construction has slowed down in Montreal, it is due to the high price of lots and also to inflation that has affected those lots since 1957.
Well, this is the content of this builders' report under the title:
A Gold Mine.
It is said that the convention:
Contended that speculation upon building sites was a real gold mine for those who exercise it, exactly because it does not require expensive work nor is it subject to taxation. It pointed out that it is done on a large scale all through this country and that it is responsible for most of the numerous problems arising from many home building projects.
Une mine d'or.
Supply-Public Works
He explained that, due to this speculation, several towns are going right now through an abnormal and very expensive expansion. He remains convinced that this situation can and must be corrected through the adoption of some taxation procedure.
I do hope that the minister will agree that the report issued at the builders convention makes sense and if he is interested he could get a copy and consider it. That may suggest to him means of stopping the inflation of lot prices so that all Canadians may eventually possess their own homes.
