speechtext: In reply to the hon. member, may I say that the number of housing starts in Montreal in 1960 was 16,345 and in 1961, it was 17,204.

In rising to say a few words on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Public Works I should like, first of all, to commend the minister on the hard work he has done in the department and on the sympathetic hearing he has given us. Often we have had to lay a rigid case before him, and sometimes, when we did not have all the facts, he turned us away until we did. But I must say when we had a good case and had the people behind us he was always sympathetic toward the provision of anything that was needed in the constituency.
In this regard I was interested in references made by the opposition to patronage. It seemed to me that every time an hon. member who supported the government got something for his riding it was considered patronage. I suggest that if opposition members followed the example of many of us on the government side, worked a lot harder for their constituencies and talked a lot less in this house, the people in their ridings would be a lot better off.
There are three items in the estimates which are of particular interest and concern to me. One has to do with the wharf at Berens River, provision for which is in the estimates this year in the amount of $65,000. I might say that a request for a wharf at Berens River has been made year after year, always failling upon deaf ears. But there was something new added last year. I may say that I have made a request for such a wharf on a number of occasions since I was elected a member of this house and I was happy to see that these representations have been successful this year.

Supply-Public Works
Berens River is an isolated community on lake Winnipeg. There are no roads to it, and those who live there must depend on air and water transport. There has been a Hudson Bay wharf there for a number of years but this has been condemned. Whenever we have sent engineers in to decide what to do about a wharf they found that some of the people wanted it on one side of the river and others wanted it on the other side; they never seemed to be able to make up their minds. Well, this little community of 125 families formed a community development association. They have an Indian reserve there, and most of the people are metis. But since they formed this little group last year they have received $20,000 to clear an air strip so that planes can land during the break up and freeze up seasons. This air strip will also serve as a hay field so that they can grow hay for cattle during the summer.
I had the pleasure of visiting Berens River a few months ago to inspect the old wharf and I was received very kindly by this committee, which has now presented a united front. That made it much easier for a member of parliament to present their case to the minister and I thank them very much for their co-operation in this regard. Here is a small community which has shown what a small community can do if the people work together. I have mentioned that $20,000 was spent last year on an air strip. A pulpwood co-operative has been formed this year and about $40,000 will be received from pulpwood under this scheme. This will provide employment in the area.
Last year, too, this isolated community which was in dire need of some health facilities received a $50,000 nursing station located there from which public health nursing can be carried on into the north. Indeed, the northern area of my riding which is extremely isolated reminds me of that series of television programs entitled "The Flying Doctor". We have that type of service in my area.
A few years back we were also fortunate enough to have established at Little Grand Rapids a $41,000 nursing station.
It has been impossible to build a road northward along the eastern shore of lake Winnipeg. Under the roads to resources program we received $1.5 million to extend roads into the remote areas. However, the terrain is such that it is impossible to build roads northward; therefore they mostly run eastward toward the Ontario boundary. As a result of this wharves along the lake are very important from the standpoint of transportation and as a means of providing a livelihood to the fishermen.

In the last few years improvements have been made in several villages along the eastern shore of lake Winnipeg. There was a wharf extension at Princess harbour which cost $7,700. Some dredging was done at Pigeon point which cost $5,500. There was some rock blasting in the harbour and dredging at Rapid Point which came to approximately $10,000.
We have had problems with regard to the locks at St. Andrews on the Red river because of the low level of water. As a result there has been a terrific odour. Of course, the city of Winnipeg is largely responsible for this. However, the Department of Public Works has been most co-operative in trying to alleviate the situation.
The locks at Lockport require an expenditure of approximately $50,000 a year for maintenance and operation. In the last three or four years it has been found necessary to build a retaining wall because of the nature of the soil in the area which causes the banks of the river to slide in. With building the retaining wall, painting the bridge and undertaking various other projects an expenditure of approximately $93,000 was made.
We have three canalmen at Lockport. They are the only canalmen in Canada who come under the Department of Public Works. Complaints have been received to the effect that they would like to be put in the same category as the other canalmen across Canada. I would ask the minister to give this consideration, if possible. They feel they have been discriminated against in some manner. Although they have been extended sympathy and their working conditions have been improved somewhat, they feel they would like to come under the Department of Transport as do all other canalmen in Canada. Of course, the civil service commission is involved and we have not received too much co-operation from that body.
In North Kildonan we have a suburban area which like all other suburbs of major cities witnesses the construction of approximately 200 and 300 new homes every year. Nearly all these homes have been constructed under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans. Most of the people in the area appreciate the action of the government in increasing maximum mortgage funds available and amending the qualifications of eligibility.
The mushrooming of the suburban area has created a number of problems and led to new necessities. One of them is a postal service. I was glad to see in the estimates this year provision for a postal letter carrier depot to be constructed in East Kildonan on the border of North Kildonan which would serve both areas. I believe the value of this depot would be approximately $65,000.

With respect to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation let me say this. A year or two ago in this house we had a great debate about the Whiteshell nuclear research establishment. The Leader of the Opposition was very persistent in attempting to have this establishment located in his own riding. Members of the C.C.F. group urged that it be located at Elliot Lake. Progress has been made at Whiteshell. Approximately $1.5 million was spent there last year and approximately $4 million will be spent this year. Of that sum approximately $1 million will be spent by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in constructing the new town site at Pinawa. To date at that townsite three land clearing contracts have been let by C.M.H.C. in the amount of $61,130 and three contracts have been let for sewage and water supply and for road bases which total a little more than $1 million. I believe an additional $1 million will be spent at the town-site in the coming year. This will provide a great deal of employment in the area. We expect that approximately 500 men will be employed there.
That brings to mind the often misquoted statement made by the Prime Minister in Prince Albert on February 14, 1958 when he said that no man or woman would suffer unnecessarily from unemployment in Canada as long as they could be helped by public works. This is but one example of how the national policy of the Conservative government is working and how this party is trying to spread public works across the nation to provide equality of opportunity.
Here is Springfield, an area 300 miles long and 150 miles wide. When a C.C.F. member represented the constituency not one public works project was undertaken. Many pages of Hansard were filled by the hon. member but not one project commenced while he was the member for that riding. Then the Liberals represented the riding for 22 years. The Liberal representatives did not talk very much but they also did not accomplish very much. As far as I can ascertain only one or two buildings were constructed in the constituency between 1935 and 1957. Here was a great area neglected. Ninety per cent of the young people of that area had to seek opportunities elsewhere. Today for the first time they can find employment with the research establishment. Not just the ordinary labouring man can find employment at the construction site, but the brilliant young people attending universities will find an employment outlet at this research establishment.
It was interesting to note that when the Leader of the Opposition made his request that this establishment not go to Manitoba he mentioned as a reason the fact that there
Supply-Public Works
would be unemployment at Elliot Lake. Many of the young people in my constituency were working at Elliot Lake. I think it would be very nice to have something to offer them in Manitoba. After all, approximately $300 million has already been spent in Ontario by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
This project is welcomed in my riding by people of all political denominations. I may say the Leader of the Opposition will receive a rare reception if he ever shows himself in Springfield.
Recently we have had a swap deal with the United States under which the Pine Tree radar stations now come under Canadian jurisdiction. We heard some criticism from the opposition about this. Here is another instance where C.M.H.C. has been able to step in and look into the matter of housing for this radar station which is now called the Beausejour R.C.A.F. station. When it was occupied by the United States it was operated of course, as a foreign base. There were fewer married men, and many lived in trailers. Now that Canada has taken over the base there has been a great demand for expansion in the area to bring it up to normal requirements for a domestic base. In the last couple of years $795,000 was spent there. We expect that $1 million, approximately, will be spent on housing this year. I believe that the Department of Public Works through C.M.H.C. will be asked to administer housing in the area.
A great deal of employment has been created in the area. The staff at the base has been increased substantially and employment will increase when C.M.H.C. undertakes to provide housing. In this regard I should like to say to the minister-and this is also a decision for the Department of National Defence-I hope the town of Beausejour and village of Lac du Bonnet might be given consideration for part of this housing. I believe approximately 100 homes will be required. Of course there is the other side to the story and that is that with this lovely new town of Pinawa going up, it would be nice to have housing situated there, and to have some consideration given to this matter. Pinawa is located on the lake. There is an attractive summer resort area there and it will have all the modern facilities of any town. It will be a showplace for Manitoba.
I forgot to say also that this summer at Lockport we will continue the extension of the retaining wall. I think there has been a vote of $10,000 for that purpose.
In Springfield we have something like 3,500 Indians. As I said before, we have put up a service for them something like the flying doctor service. In this regard the

Supply-Public Works
Department of Public Works, in conjunction with the Department of National Health and Welfare, put up a nurses' residence last year which cost $112,000. I understand that plans are under way to amalgamate the Indian affairs hospital along with that in the pulp and paper town of Pine Falls and that something in the neighbourhood of $400,000 will be spent there in the coming year.
We have in our riding beautiful Fort Garry, the old stone fort, which is one of the few forts remaining intact. We hope by 1967 it will be our own showplace in Manitoba. This was the fort that was locked to visitors when I was elected. I raised this matter. I might say that last year something like 50,000 visitors signed the guest book. We have put two guides in. This year we are building there a museum that will cost something like $50,000.
I think that just goes to show you what a member can do if he works hard for his constituency.
Here was an area that had been neglected since confederation. When you walked into it, you found it was an area that was barren. There were no roads to speak of. There were no opportunities. The young people, as soon as they got out of school, were obliged to go and seek their livelihood in the great city of Winnipeg. Many of them found their way to Toronto and to the east, many of them going to the United States and so forth. So we saw that under the Liberals at least 50 per cent of the young people in the province were leaving and as far as the rural areas were concerned probably it was more like 90 per cent. Now, under this national development policy of this government through these public works and other projects we are trying to keep our young people at home with their families, where they can get married and raise families and find some opportunity. That is what our policy is designed for, namely, to treat all areas alike and to bring those that are underdeveloped up to the standards we can see elsewhere.
I could go on to talk about a large number of other things. There is the trans-Canada highway that runs through my riding. Several million dollars have been spent on it. There is a south and north perimenter road around the city of Winnipeg. The south perimeter road, of course, has been proceeded with and is being widened to four lanes, but in the north perimeter road we have not yet reached the stage of building the bridge across the river. I might say that, with the traffic pattern in the suburbs of Winnipeg, there is an increasing demand for this bridge and that the municipalities in the area are very much concerned about it. There is an oil refinery 
on one side and there is a great deal of traffic from the east to the west and from the west to the east as far as gravel trucks are concerned. Some of the best gravel is found on the east side. There is a great deal of crossing the river because of the mushrooming of the suburbs. The traffic patterns indicate that this bridge should be proceeded with at the earliest possible moment. This, of course, is not the decision for the federal government. It is rather a decision for the provincial government. However, I think the people in the area should know that we are very much concerned about the matter and that we are certainly going to see that this bridge is built at the earliest possible moment.
As I say, the Department of Public Works has been most kind to us. I might also say that it was not very easy to get all these things. It was not a matter of writing to the minister and saying that I want this or I want that. If he gave it, he wanted to know the reason for it. Often it was with the cooperation of municipalities in the area, and other groups there that we could bring the need before the people.
I think this record of accomplishment in Springfield is a record of which I can be proud. I am willing to place it against that of any other member of parliament who ever represented the riding and against all the members of parliament who represented the Liberal party in the riding since confederation. I should like to stack it up and see how it matches. I think it would match up very well. This area had been neglected for so long both by the provincial Liberals and the federal Liberals that it was inevitable that much of this had to be done, and we were the party that came out and did it. There were many things that the Liberals said could not be done. However, with a little bit of conscientious hard work, we did them.
I do not want to drag this discussion out, Mr. Chairman. I have a great deal more that I could say but I think most of it would not come under this department. In refutation of the member of the New Democratic party who talked about patronage, I should just like to say that if that little group over there did a little bit more hard work, a little bit less talking and became a little bit more concerned with individuals in the places in the riding, they too could have a record like this one to show their people.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Vancouver East,

I wish to ask the minister this question. In his remarks a few minutes ago he gave statistics for the condition in

Montreal in 1961. I wish to ask him whether he was giving the figures for Montreal only or for metropolitan Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: For metropolitan Montreal.
That is different.

Because I think it is the right thing to do, Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to thank the Minister of Public Works and his deputy, General Young, for their courtesy in answering in connection with any problems I have raised with them since the last introduction of item No. 1 of the Department of Public Works. I am one of the relatively few members in the House of Commons who can rise in his place and speak on item No. 1 of the Department of Public Works in a particular way as I have not a federal building in Vancouver East. As a matter of fact, to my knowledge there is no federal public works expenditure in the entire set-up of Vancouver East. That is why I say I am one of the relatively few who can rise in his place and speak on this item when there is nothing spent in his riding. What may surprise you, Mr. Chairman, and the minister is that on behalf of Vancouver East and as its member here I am not asking for a federal building or for a post office or for any expenditure his department can make in my riding itself. I happen to represent a riding which is basically residential. In it there are only a few secondary industries and the harbour front.
What I have to say under this item is said on behalf of the city of Vancouver because what affects Vancouver has a definite effect on over 100,000 men, women and children who live within the boundaries of the federal constituency of Vancouver East. There are three matters which are of major concern, I believe, in Vancouver which either come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works or upon which he can give advice.
The first matter I want to raise is one on which I admit there might be a split jurisdiction or perhaps the matter might not come under the minister at all. He will tell me about that. I refer to the harbour development in Vancouver. Vancouver, as the minister knows, is the third largest city in Canada. It is not only the major western port of Canada but one of the most important western ports in North America. With the expansion of trade westward, Vancouver is now in the position where the harbour facilities are completely underdeveloped. If my memory is correct, Mr. Chairman, it has been some 20 years since one of the major harbour facilities owned by the Canadian Pacific was burnt down and it has never been replaced. Any of you who follow the western newspapers undoubtedly saw pictures in the past few 26207-1-904
Supply-Public Works
weeks showing ocean-going liners waiting at anchor in the inner harbour for a spot to load and unload cargo.
Vancouver East and Vancouver Centre are the boundaries of the harbour areas of Vancouver. One half of the harbour of Vancouver is in my riding. I would ask the Minister of Public Works, therefore, if it comes under his jurisdiction in any way whatever, and if there is any planning for federal government participation in harbour development in the city of Vancouver. I am afraid that perhaps the authority of the Minister of Public Works may only extend up to the tidal high-water mark. However, because of the prime importance of Vancouver to Canada, I hope he does not mind my raising the problem now. I am certain he is cognizant of it. If he has jurisdiction, then he will tell us of any planning. If, as I am led to believe, his authority does not extend beyond the tidal shore, he may have some influence with his colleagues in the cabinet.
The next matter, Mr. Chairman, I know comes completely within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works. I am thinking of senior citizens housing, something of which I have been concerned and which I have been interested for many years. This is a major problem in the city of Vancouver. I know all cities and all provinces have this problem of housing for senior citizens. I know from facts, figures and studies that the city of Vancouver has the major problem because, situated as it is on the Pacific coast and having no extremes of heat or humidity in summer or freezing weather in winter, it has the greatest percentage of senior citizens of any major city in Canada. These people do not live their lives in British Columbia. They come to British Columbia in later years of life as old age pensioners or superannuates. The Vancouver city council is cognizant of the situation. The Vancouver city council, under the leadership of His Worship A. T. Alsbury, has been doing everything possible to work in cooperation with the province and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make homes and apartments available for our senior citizens at rents which they can afford to pay.
I should like to ask the minister what his policy is, how far he is prepard to go and how far he has told Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to go in co-operating with councils and provincial governments in supplying homes for our senior citizens. You may ask, Mr. Chairman, why I put the question in that way. I do so, sir, because of the communications I have received from the Vancouver city council, from His Worship A.T. Alsbury and communications from Dr. Bates of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. These communications have led

Supply-Public Works
me to believe that for some reason or other Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is blocking the desire of the city of Vancouver to extend aid to its senior citizens. I know, and I want to be the first to admit, that there are a number of projects under way authorized by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I answer the hon. member? I am very glad he has raised any matter that is in his mind. I can reassure him that not only Dr. Bates but all the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are anxious and willing and have been cooperating with the officials of Vancouver in an earnest effort to get proper housing for the elderly. Anybody who is not politically prejudiced I think would be very happy to admit that. I know, of course, the hon. member for Vancouver East is not being political, he is just telling what somebody has told him. He wanted an answer, and I am happy to have been able to give him this answer.

I am very glad that the Minister of Public Works has said I am not politically prejudiced on this matter. I am sorry, though, that he said I am telling something I have been told. This infers I am basing my remarks on rumour. I should like to say I am making them on the basis of information supplied me by the Vancouver city council over the signature of his worship the mayor. This informs me that over 12 months ago the city and the provincial government passed authorization for construction of 300 additional units in the city of Vancouver. I am in receipt of a further communication to the effect that this program has been dropped because of no action, no authorization, after 12 months from central mortgage and housing. I think you will agree with me, Mr. Chairman, that as a member for the city of Vancouver and having that information over the name of his worship, the mayor of Vancouver, I should take it as pretty factual information. Moreover, I shall say I also have that over the name of Mr. Bates in a recent letter to me.
Why is it being held up? They state they are not quite certain whether there will be the need, or at least that is my interpretation of the letter. They want to wait until the 400 now under construction are completed. May I point out to the Minister of Public Works that the last analytical figures show that inside of 24 months the requirements for senior citizens will be approximately 5,000 of the type of homes that Vancouver wants to proceed with at an accelerated rate.
I know the interest of the Minister of Public Works in this matter. I know all that has


been done by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Good heavens, I am the one man who should know it because my father and myself started the first of this type of house construction in Canada and we could never have done it without central mortgage and housing and their mortgages at very low rates of interest. I know what central mortgage and housing has done, but I say there is much more to be done, and I know the minister by supplementary estimates brings in additional millions of dollars for central mortgage. That is why I cannot understand why the city of Vancouver, the third largest city in Canada, and the province of British Columbia have been waiting for 12 months to go ahead with something that is blocked by central mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would read Dr. Bates' letter.

I would be very glad, sir. It will take me five or 10 minutes to get it down from my office but I shall be glad to read the three letters to the house, one from Vancouver council, one I received three weeks ago from Dr. Bates and the letter which I sent him two days ago furthering my plea to authorize the additional construction of senior citizens housing in Vancouver. In view of what the minister has just said I will not say anything more on that now but, sir, when we come to deal with that particular item I shall have all the documentation on this matter and will accept the invitation of the minister to read it to the house.
There is another item of major importance to us in Vancouver on which I would like to make a personal plea to the Minister of Public Works. I was most interested in the speech from the throne, part of which made reference to the government negotiating with the province of Quebec to remove the tolls on two bridges. That is a most worthy endeavour and I sincerely hope they are successful in removing those tolls because in this day and age toll bridges and toll highways are a curse on modem civilization and modem transportation.
Because of the peculiar circumstances in which the speech from the throne says that at this particular session, at this particular time, the government is going to negotiate with the province of Quebec about the removal of tolls on two bridges, and because of what that means to the great city of Montreal and the people in its environs, I would like to ask the minister: please will you take a look at the city of Vancouver in the province of British Columbia?
In Vancouver proper we have one third of the entire population of British Columbia; in

Vancouver metropolitan area we have almost one half of the entire population of British Columbia, and we are a city, an island, surrounded by toll bridges. Unless we travel via the Pattullo bridge at New Westminster, half a million of us cannot get out of Vancouver without paying a toll unless we go 62 miles up to the city of Mission and cross there on a combined road and railroad bridge. This is the list: First Narrows, a toll bridge; Second Narrows, two toll bridges; Oak Street, a toll bridge and the Deas tunnel, a toll tunnel. They are now putting up a new bridge at Port Mann, another toll bridge. I repeat, the only way we can get out of Vancouver without paying tolls is over the Pattullo bridge.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
I understand him to be laying it down as a self-evident fact that toll bridges are a bad thing and ought to be disposed of.
Yes.

I wonder if that is necessarily so. I have not a fixed view on the matter but it does seem to me that where bridges are put up for the benefit of certain people it is fair that they should pay for them, and not the taxpayers at large. I do not want to inject myself into the hon. member's speech, but he stated that as a self-evident fact. I am not able to see it, but at the moment I am not able to make any effective argument against it.

I think with the taxation on gasoline, the taxation on tires, the taxation on automobiles, the taxation on oil and the taxation on licences it is a curse that in a city like Vancouver, with a population of half a million people, we cannot get out of that city without paying a toll.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I would point out, Mr. Chairman, we have nothing to do with tolls. We have no tolls.
The only route we can get out of Vancouver without paying tolls is over the Pattullo bridge-
On a point of order-
-because the government named the Pattullo bridge as a highway on the trans-Canada highway.

On a point of order; the Minister of Public Works has raised a very valid point. Tolls are not the responsibility of the Department of Public Works.
Supply-Public Works
If that is so then I would like to know why the throne speech says this government is going to work with Montreal and Quebec to remove the tolls on two bridges in Montreal.

We debated the throne
speech for eight days.

I am discussing the point you raised. If I am now out of order in discussing the matter of tolls then that sentence in the throne speech was out of order. I am glad that the government is entering into negotiations with the province of Quebec to remove tolls on two bridges in the city of Montreal but I would say "Please, Mr. Minister, will you not give some consideration to entering into negotiations with the province of British Columbia for the removal of tolls on those damned bridges that surround us"? Of course, we have one bridge which is free. It was built in 1936. I refer to the Pattullo bridge. The time-
The Depuly Chairman: Order. I have been allowing the hon. member a great deal of leeway on this particular point. The minister interjected briefly to state that his department was in no way responsible for the tolls that are charged on these particular bridges. For that reason I find it difficult to relate what the hon. member is saying to item No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Public Works. The hon. member has made his case as a result of the leeway I have allowed him on the matter, and perhaps he could now turn to something else.

That is not necessary, Mr. Chairman; you have already given me the answer because you said I have made my case in appealing to the Minister of Public Works. We know from the debate on the speech from the throne that negotiations are being entered into with the government of Quebec, and I would ask the minister to please enter into negotiations with the government of British Columbia, not only with regard to the Pattullo bridge-that is all settled-but on the other bridges so that tolls may be removed and we will not be an island surrounded by bridges, having to pay out of our pockets for entering or leaving our own city, the third largest in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should first like to congratulate the minister upon his excellent statement with regard to housing, public works, the trans-Canada highway and the national capital commission, I should like to raise two points in connection with the criticisms of hon. members of the opposition. The first matter

Supply-Public Works
concerns the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming about patronage in public works.
I hope that the minister in his remarks in this debate will make it perfectly clear that contracts for public buildings are put out to tender and the lowest tender gets the contract. The other point concerns the remarks of the hon. member for Levis. His irrelevant attack upon the minister with regard to highways, and so on, was just a way to conceal the good things that have been done by this government in the fields of public works and housing.
I should first like to dwell for a moment upon the broad housing policies of the Conservative government. I think this is one area in which we can take a great deal of pride for what this government has done in the past four and a half years.
I should like to dwell upon the financial situation and cite the metropolitan area of Hamilton, Ontario, as an example of the dynamic way in which this government has dealt with the housing situation in the country. An hon. Liberal member said there was a shortage of money in 1956 and 1957. This is the fact. The lending institutions across the country entered the commercial and industrial lending fields, thereby drying up the lower interest yield on mortgage money for housing and forcing this government to enter the house lending business on a large scale.
I think the Liberal regime was well aware of this drying up of capital in the latter part of 1956 and the early part of 1957, and I think they should have taken a lead in starting direct lending well in advance of June 10, 1957. However, I am sure it was not their intention to let the people know of the economic report that was concealed, which indicated the cyclical decline of housing construction and a forecast of a further decline in the future.
I should also like to comment upon the fact that the approved lending institutions in Hamilton loaned $63 million from 1957 to the end of 1961. As far as limited dividend corporation loans are concerned, in that period $3,738,172 were loaned in Hamilton. This is in regard to privately owned limited dividend corporations which are providing homes for senior citizens. With regard to direct loans by C.M.H.C. to private individuals and private lending corporations, a total of $31,170,472 were loaned.
I am sure that the ambitious city of Hamilton has been greatly assisted in their progressive construction in housing, with loans totalling $97,936,000. This figure excludes direct lending from trust or insurance companies not on approved lending lists, and conventional loans. I am sure that if this

government had not gone into the lending field in a direct way, in the way it did when it started lending $150 million directly and eventually brought the figure up to $2 billion, many builders in this country would have gone bankrupt through lack of funds.
I think the Minister of Public Works, his department and C.M.H.C. should be commended for doing a very fine job in this regard. Next I should like to talk about Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation. I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Vancouver east say that C.M.H.C. has been blocking loans for senior citizens homes-
They blocked one in Vancouver.

I gathered form the intensity of the hon. member's attack that he was very disturbed about these loans that were proposed to be blocked by C.M.H.C. In Hamilton loans applications that have been put through our city council, they have received the acknowledgement of the federal government, have passed through C.M.H.C. in a matter of days and in fact these dwellings have been built and people are living in them. I am speaking of senior citizens dwellings, limited dividend loans incomes ranging between $3,000 and $4,200 a year, and federal-provincial housing for those with income levels from $2,950 and less a year to $5,800 a year. With these income levels people cannot afford today to buy their own home because of the lack of capital, and with their low earnings they cannot acquire a mortgage.
In the city of Hamilton we have a very large program in this respect. There are some 1,200 federal-provincial homes in my riding. This program is operating very effectively, with a small waiting list. As far as limited dividend private corporation loans in Hamilton are concerned, the list is completely filled with people within the proper incomes. There is also a small waiting list in this category.
As far as urban renewal expansion and development is concerned, in the city of Hamilton, as in other parts of the country, I think this government is very aware of all the ramifications and problems that we are going to run into. Hamilton took a lead by setting up an urban renewal committee. This committee was designed to get the ball rolling in Hamilton as far as urban renewal was concerned. The initial impetus in regard to urban renewal must come from the municipalities. The federal government and C.M.H.C. can give assistance and provide people who are able to go out and help, but initially the initial effort must come from the municipalities.

The federal government is interested in a person who may be uprooted because of urban renewal, and it is of the utmost importance that the federal government should look after the individual to ensure that he is protected in every way and will not be thrown out of his home in a very haphazard way if it is blighted. In the past 18 months Hamilton has undertaken the clearance study of 278 acres. This program is under consideration at the present time by the provincial authority in Toronto. There are problems which will arise because of this redevelopment. One of the problems is, not that the federal government has not dealt in a forward looking way with urban renewal but the problems that arise in this regard that may be of interest to the committee. The act now states that urban renewal is for the clearance of slum or blight areas, the relocation of homes and the development of new housing accommodation, but there is no section in the act which indicates that in an area of blight or semi-deterioration where a large area is cleared, where schools and recreational facilities are needed, the clearance of these areas for these facilities comes under the National Housing Act. I would hope that the officials of C.M.H.C. would look into the aspects of an integral part of the redevelopment of certain areas so that not only housing could be used for the redevelopment but schools and recreation areas. Possibly there could be a relocation of traffic through the tearing down of blighted areas so that we could go even further in the vast scope of urban renewal.
The next point I should like to deal with for a moment concerns the cost of land in the country as a whole. Everyone knows it is going up and up. But I want to point out one thing which this government has done, and I think it has a direct relationship to the cost of land. In the bill which was passed here some 18 months ago that made available sewer loans to the municipalities, hidden in this type of legislation is a thought to reduce the cost of land. In the constituency that I represent we were very fortunate that out of $40 million of initial loans for sewerage receptacles and sewage disposal plants we had over $2 million, showing the progressive way in which the city council of Hamilton is taking advantage of this legislation.
But there is a larger scope in land servicing. The reason that land costs are high is that services have been creeping steadily out of the centre of the city, thereby putting a high premium price on that land near where the services are being constructed. Under the legislation which was passed some time ago providing for the availability of long term
Supply-Public Works
sewer loans to the municipalities, the legislation allowed for servicing large tracks of land, where desirable, so as to open up vast tracks of land, thereby putting a glut on the market and forcing the price down because of the number of lots that would be available. This is an example of the supply and demand theory.
I hope that the federal government on March 31, 1963 will take a look at the long term program of federal sewage loans. I think this will help the cost of land and do a good job in the long run.
In Hamilton as a whole we have had practically everything in the housing field. We have had federal-provincial housing, limited dividend lending, direct corporation lending, approved lending, sewer loans and even land assembly. There are a number of pro and con thoughts on land assembly. There are many builders, in private enterprise, who believe in land assembly and some who are private enterprisers who do not believe in it. But 540 lots in Hamilton south were done two years ago. I do not want to argue the pros and cons of land assembly, but I do know there are 500 homes in my constituency that are there and built. It is a beautiful survey. It is a pleasure for parents to bring up their children in this type of assembly because the municipality has built beautiful schools and park areas have been correlated in this development.
I should like to congratulate C.M.H.C. on the sale of mortgages to private institutions. I think this is a good thing and I hope it will continue in the future.
The next subject I should like to dwell on is over-all public works as pertaining to Hamilton south and Hamilton as a whole. Hamilton, as I am sure everyone knows, is a progessive city. It has the third largest tonnage harbour in Canada although it is a great distance from the sea. The federal government has recognized this fact, and from the point of view of harbour expenditure I think it is second to none in relation to the population of the area. So far as dredging is concerned, since 1957 there has been some $2,245,000 spent on dredging down in the Hamilton area to keep the channel open. So far as public works are concerned, Hamilton is a conservative stronghold. We have all Conservative members and we work as a team to develop the harbour and to develop the public works. There will be some-
Oh, oh.

If the hon. member who represents one of the Ontario constituencies-I believe it is Timmins- would like to get up and contribute to the debate and tell us what he thinks of housing,

I am sure we would be happy to hear from him.
As far as public buildings are concerned we were fortunate that a long time ago post offices and other public buildings were built, but a little over a million dollars worth of additions have been done in the past short while.
I should like to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Wentworth. I am sorry he is not in the house tonight; I think he has another engagement. For many years in his constituency the entrance of the Hamilton harbour has been a very vexing point. A couple of ships ran into the old bridge and blocked the harbour for some time. Through the persistence of this hon. member I believe a new low level bridge costing $5,122,960 will be opened this year. I think it is really due to the personal efforts of this member that this is being done.
As far as the harbour and river facilities estimates are concerned there is provision for the expenditure of some $7,438,000 in the Hamilton area as a whole and I should like to tell the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that we are very appreciative in Hamilton not of just being given money but also very appreciative of getting the money that is developing our community into one of the strongest economic units in the country in the whole area of housing, and harbour and bridge construction. I think it is proving that the Conservative government is on the right track. It has not left Hamilton behind.
I cannot stress too much the importance of the minister's taking up with C.M.H.C. the sections of the National Housing Act with regard to urban renewal. I have sat on the urban renewal committee in Hamilton as the federal representative and I have learned a great deal from this, but I find that there are some loopholes which I think can be cured very easily so that when a city or municipality is designing an urban renewal area they can go into the whole ramifications of schools, recreation facilities, churches and so on, along with housing and apartment dwellings in that area.
I should like to take this opportunity of saying that C.M.H.C. in the constituency which I represent and in Hamilton as a whole has done a great job and the co-operation they have given, in an unprejudiced and unpolitical way to, I think, every member Of the house is appreciated. They should be congratulated, and I hope they will continue their good work in the future.

I should like to begin my remarks in this debate by expressing my thanks to the minister and his staff for the very kind and, for the most part, sympathetic consideration they have given to the problems
[Mr. McDonald (Hamilton South) .1

I have brought before them on behalf of my constituents. I should like to take this opportunity also of expressing my appreciation to the staff of the minister's department, both the senior officials here and the officials in the district office in our province. They have always been most co-operative and most sympathetic and have gone out of their way on many occasions to do everything possible to alleviate the problems that I have had to bring before them. The minister is very fortunate in having such competent and devoted officials at the disposal of his department.
When I listened to the minister opening the debate on this item I must say he sounded to me much more like the minister for housing than the Minister of Public Works. Housing is of course, a very important activity in the minister's department and also in the economic life of our country. Housing is one of the very best ways of priming the pump when our economy slows down. The minister has told us that a great deal has been done in that direction under this government. As I listened to the minister it was not clear to me whether the aim of the government's housing policy was to create jobs or to build needed homes. One can understand that under the economic conditions which we have experienced during the past few years a delicate balance has perhaps had to be achieved between the two.
In a free enterprise country when a government has to go so deeply into the housing business there is raised in my mind a question as to whether the economic and fiscal policies followed by the government are sound. The prime purpose of every national government is to create a climate in which private enterprise can operate to fill the needs of the people. Housing is a legitimate function of private enterprise. If it is impossible for them to carry out this normal function I think we should take a second look to see whether this is due to our failure to provide the proper climate and whether the fiscal policies pursued by the government have something to do with it.
The minister took great pride in what this government has accomplished in the field of housing. I cannot share his enthusiasm in this respect. For a national policy which is designed to apply to all parts of the nation and to treat every part of the nation alike, the figures the minister placed on Hansard this afternoon certainly show this is not being done.
He told us that in the country as a whole aggregate loans under C.M.H.C. totalled $3,271 million. Then he went on to tell us that 50 per cent of this amount had gone to one province. Out of the aggregate a total of $1,600

million went to Ontario alone, while loans in all the Atlantic provinces totalled only $120 million.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, not the
amount available.

These are the figures the minister placed on the record. As I understood the minister, of the aggregate of $3,271 million a total of $1,600 million went to Ontario and $120 million went to the Atlantic provinces.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They could have had more.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member knows very well that we have to receive applications. After all, we do not go about soliciting applications. Unless the provinces make applications on their own through the various channels there is nothing we can do about it. Surely there is no criticism of that. We make a special point of doing all we can to assist the Atlantic provinces.

I quite understand that, Mr. Chairman, and I was not criticizing the minister. I was criticizing the way the policy has worked out in one part of Canada compared with another. We know that people must apply. If they do not apply in the Atlantic provinces it is because they cannot afford to apply. That is what I am complaining about. The great national policy, so called, of which the minister is so proud actually operates to favour the rich provinces. A wealthy province like Ontario can take advantage of it but poor provinces like the Atlantic provinces are not in a position to take advantage of it. That is why the people of the Atlantic provinces do not apply. They would apply just as readily as the people of Ontario if they could afford to do so.
I believe a national policy applied to the whole nation should be designed to operate in such a way as to take into account the economic differences in the various regions and not to favour the rich at the expense of the poor.
Even if we considered it as the minister seemed to do this afternoon as a means of creating employment, the need in the Atlantic provinces is much greater than in Ontario. The minister of finance for Ontario has said the employment situation is better in Ontario than in Canada as a whole and better than in the United States. Let us understand that that is not so in the Atlantic provinces. Approximately 13 per cent of our people are out of work now and probably 25 or 30 per cent of them will be out of work before the winter is over.

I am not in a position to give the numbers of the bills with which we will deal on

Monday, but on Monday and Tuesday we will deal with legislation. We will commence by taking up some of the items on the order paper standing in the name of the Minister of Finance. I will detail them tomorrow when the house rises.

shall-I am amazed that we did not finish them today in view of the friendly position which the Minister of Public Works has taken on television and in this house-following their completion tomorrow morning we shall then go on with northern affairs tomorrow afternoon.
